Surah 83: Al-Mutaffifin (The Defrauders)

Makkan, and its verses number 36 [revealed after al-Ankabut, and it is the last surah revealed in Makkah].

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

At-Tatfif (defrauding): diminishing (al-bakhs) in measuring and weighing, because what is diminished is trivial (tafif) and contemptible. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, its people were among the worst of people in measuring, so this was revealed, and they then did good measuring. [[Recorded by al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim from the narration of Yazid al-Nahwi from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]] It is also said: when he came to Madinah there was a man there known as Abu Juhaynah, who had two saa' measures: he measured with one and took measure with the other. [[Transmitted by al-Tha'labi from al-Suddi.]]

It is also said: the people of Madinah were merchants who defrauded, and their transactions were al-munabadhah, al-mulamasah and al-mukhatarah, so this was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out and recited it to them. [[I have not found it.]] He said: "Five for five." It was asked: O Messenger of Allah, what is "five for five"? He said: "No people break a covenant except that Allah gives their enemy power over them; they do not rule by other than what Allah has revealed except that poverty spreads among them; immorality does not appear among them except that death spreads among them; they do not defraud in measure except that they are denied plant growth and seized by years of drought; and they do not withhold zakat except that rain is withheld from them." [[Recorded by al-Hakim from the narration of Abdullah ibn Buraydah from his father, raised to the Prophet: "No people broke a covenant..." the hadith; in its chain is Bishr ibn al-Muhajir, about whom there is discussion. Also by way of Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from Abdullah ibn Amr, raised, similar.]]

And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: he passed by a man weighing saffron who had tilted the scale, and said to him: "Establish the weight with justice, then tilt it afterward as you wish." It is as if he ordered him first to level it, so that he would become accustomed to it and distinguish the obligatory from the voluntary.

And from Ibn Abbas: "You, the non-Arabs, have been entrusted with two matters, by which those before you were destroyed: the measure and the balance." He specified non-Arabs because they combine measuring and weighing together, whereas the two were separated in the two sanctuaries: the people of Makkah weighed and the people of Madinah measured.

And from Ibn Umar: he would pass by a seller and say to him: "Fear Allah and give full measure, for the defrauders will be made to stand on the Day of Resurrection before the majesty of the Most Merciful, until the sweat reaches to their bridles."

And from Ikrimah: "I testify that every measurer and weigher is in the Fire." It was said to him: "Your son is a measurer or weigher." He said: "I testify that he is in the Fire."

And from Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him: "Do not seek needs from those whose provision is in the heads of measures and the tongues of scales."

Since their measuring from people was a measuring that harms them, and it wrongs them, he replaced "ʿalā" (upon) in place of "min" (from) to indicate that. [[Mahmud said: "Since their measuring upon people was a measuring that harms them... etc." Ahmad says: there is no contention in this, and this speaker does not make the pronoun indicate direct performance, nor is there any indication in it of that. Rather the composition of the speech takes this form: when measuring is from others, they exact it fully; when measuring is from them specifically, they diminish it, whether they perform it themselves or not. This is the most orderly and best composition, and Allah knows best. What shows you that the pronoun does not confer direct performance of the act is that you may say: "The rulers are the ones who establish the penalties, not the common people," and you do not mean that they carry it out with their own hands, but rather that the doing of it is from them specifically.]]

It is also permissible that "ʿalā" be connected to yastawfūn, and the object be placed before the verb to convey exclusivity, meaning: they exact in full from people specifically; as for themselves, they exact in full for themselves.

Al-Farra' said: "min" and "ʿalā" alternate in this position, because it is a right upon him; so when one says "iktaltu ʿalayka" (I took measure upon you), it is as if he said "akhadhtu mā ʿalayka" (I took what is upon you), and when one says "iktaltu minka" (I took measure from you), it is like his saying "istawaytu minka" (I exacted from you).

The pronoun in kāluhum aw wazanūhum is an objective pronoun referring to the people. There are two views: that it is intended as "kālū lahum aw wazanū lahum" (they measured for them or weighed for them), so the preposition is dropped and the verb is made to reach the pronoun directly, as the poet said:

"And I have indeed gathered for you truffles and ʿasāqil, and indeed I forbade you from the plant al-awbar."

[[Jana yataʿaddā illā li-wāḥid wa-l-thānī bi-l-lām, fa-l-aṣl: janaytu laka, fa-ḥudhifa al-jār wa-ūṣila al-ḍamīr. Aw ḍammanahu maʿnā: abaḥtuka, fa-ʿaddāhu li-humā. Al-akmuʾ: jamʿ kamaʾ, ka-aflus wa-fals, wa-huwa wāḥid al-kamʾah, wa-hiya li-nawʿ kabīr min nabāt yusammā shaḥmat al-arḍ, summiya kamʾah li-ishtihārihi bihā. Al-ʿasāqil: jamʿ ʿasqūl ka-ʿuṣfūr, wa-kāna ḥaquhu: ʿasāqīl, fa-ḥudhifat al-yāʾ li-l-wazn. Wa-qīl: innahu jamʿ ʿasqal, wa-huwa nawʿ ṣaghīr minhā jayyid abyaḍ, wa-nabāt awbar: nawʿ radīʾ minhā aswad mazghab, ka-anna ʿalayhi wabar. Wa-qīl: huwa jins ākhar yushbih al-qalqās aw al-lift. Wa-nabāt awbar: jamʿ ibn awbar, li-annahu ʿalam li-mā lā yaʿqil. Wa-al fīhi zāʾida. Wa-qāla al-Mubarrad: huwa ism jins, qāla fīhi maʿrifa, wa-al-bayt min bāb al-tamthīl mithāl ?????: man aghrā ʿalā al-ṭayyib, fa-ʿadala ilā al-khabīth, thumma yarjiʿu yatanaddamu ʿalā ʿātibatihi.]]

And "the eager one hunts you, not the generous one," in the sense of: I gathered for you, and he hunts for you. It may also be by omitting a modifier and placing the modified noun in its stead, the modifier being "the measured or the weighed." It is not valid for the pronoun to be a nominative referring to the defrauders, because the speech would then come out into a corrupt composition: the meaning would be "when they take from people they exact in full, and when they give to them they diminish," but if the pronoun refers to the defrauders it becomes like your saying: "When they take from people they exact in full, and when they themselves specifically undertake the measuring or weighing they diminish," and this is incoherent speech, because the discourse concerns the act and not the one who directly performs it. The argument for nullifying this by the script of the Mushaf, namely that the alif written after the waw of the plural is not firm in it, is weak, because the script of the Mushaf in much of it did not observe the standard rules of orthography established in the science of writing. Moreover, I have seen in manuscripts in the hands of the proficient imams this alif rejected, since it is firm neither in pronunciation nor in meaning, for the waw alone conveys the meaning of plurality; this alif was written only to distinguish the plural waw from others, as in your saying "hum lam yadʿū" and "huwa yadʿū"; whoever does not write it says the meaning suffices to distinguish them. It is narrated from Isa ibn Umar and Hamzah that they used to adopt this, that is, they make both pronouns refer to the defrauders, and they pause at the two waws, a pause by which they show what they intended.

If you say: why was it not said "aw ittazanū" (or they weigh for themselves), as was said "aw wazanūhum"? I reply: it is as if the defrauders would take only what is measured and weighed by measures, not by scales, because by measuring they could achieve full exaction and theft, for they would shake the measure and cheat in filling it; and when they gave, they measured or weighed, because they were able to diminish in both kinds together. "Yukhsirūn" means: they diminish. It is said: "khasira al-mīzān" and "akhsarahu" [[His words "it is said: khasira al-mizan" — the phrasing of al-Sihah: "khasirtu al-shay' wa-akhsartuhu: naqqastuhu." (ʿ)]].

"Alā yaẓunnu" is a strong denunciation and marvel at their condition in daring to defraud, as if they do not bring to mind nor even surmise that they will be resurrected and called to account for the weight of an atom or a mustard seed. It is narrated from Qatadah: "Give full measure, O son of Adam, as you wish full measure to be given to you, and be just as you wish justice to be done to you." And from al-Fudayl: "The diminishing of the scale is the blackening of the face on the Day of Resurrection."

And from Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: a Bedouin said to him: "You have heard what Allah said about the defrauders." He meant by this that the defrauder has incurred the great threat you have heard of; so what is your opinion of yourself, when you take the wealth of the Muslims without measure or weight?

In this denunciation and marvel, the word "zann," the description of the Day as great, the standing of people on it humbly before Allah, and His describing Himself as Lord of the worlds, is an eloquent statement of the enormity of sin and the magnitude of wrong in defrauding, and in what is like its state of injustice and abandoning the upholding of justice, and acting with equity and fairness in every taking and giving, indeed in every word and deed.

It is also said: "zann" means certainty, though the meaning mentioned is preferable. "Yawma yaqūmu" is in the accusative, governed by "mabʿūthūn." It is also read in the genitive as a substitute for "li-yawmin ʿaẓīm." And from Ibn Umar: he recited this surah, and when he reached His words "the Day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds," he wept profusely and stopped reciting what followed.

"Alā yaẓunnu" is a strong denunciation and marvel at their condition in daring to defraud, as if they do not bring to mind nor even surmise that they will be resurrected and called to account for the weight of an atom or a mustard seed. It is narrated from Qatadah: "Give full measure, O son of Adam, as you wish full measure to be given to you, and be just as you wish justice to be done to you." And from al-Fudayl: "The diminishing of the scale is the blackening of the face on the Day of Resurrection."

And from Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: a Bedouin said to him: "You have heard what Allah said about the defrauders." He meant by this that the defrauder has incurred the great threat you have heard of; so what is your opinion of yourself, when you take the wealth of the Muslims without measure or weight?

In this denunciation and marvel, the word "zann," the description of the Day as great, the standing of people on it humbly before Allah, and His describing Himself as Lord of the worlds, is an eloquent statement of the enormity of sin and the magnitude of wrong in defrauding, and in what is like its state of injustice and abandoning the upholding of justice, and acting with equity and fairness in every taking and giving, indeed in every word and deed.

It is also said: "zann" means certainty, though the meaning mentioned is preferable. "Yawma yaqūmu" is in the accusative, governed by "mabʿūthūn." And from Ibn Umar: he recited this surah, and when he reached His words "the Day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds," he wept profusely and stopped reciting what followed.

Kallā (By no means!) — a rebuke directed at them for what they were doing of cheating in measure and their heedlessness of the remembrance of the Resurrection and the Reckoning. It alerts them that this is something they must repent of and feel remorse for. Then he follows it with a threat against the wicked (fujjār) in general. The "record of the wicked" (kitāb al-fujjār) is what is written down of their deeds.

If you say: Allah has informed us that the record of the wicked is in Sijjīn, and He explained Sijjīn as "a written record" (kitāb marqūm), so it is as if it were said: their record is in a written record. What is its meaning?

I say: Sijjīn is a comprehensive book, the register of evil. Allah has recorded in it the deeds of the devils and the deeds of the disbelievers and the transgressors among jinn and humankind. It is a "written record" (kitāb marqūm), inscribed and set down in writing. Or it is a marker (muʿallam) by which whoever sees it knows that there is no good in it. So the meaning is that what is written of the deeds of the wicked is fixed in that register. It was named Sijjīn as a form (faʿīl) derived from "imprisonment" (sajn), which means confinement and constriction, because it is the cause of confinement and constriction in Hell. Or it is because it is cast down (maṭrūḥ), as has been related, beneath the seventh earth, in a desolate, dark place. It is the dwelling of Iblīs and his offspring, as a way of humiliating it and degrading it, and so that the banished devils may witness it, just as the angels brought near witness the register of good.

If you say: Is Sijjīn an adjective or a proper noun? I say: Rather, it is a proper noun (ism ʿalam) transferred from an adjective, like Ḥātim, and it is diptotic (munṣarif, i.e., it takes tanwīn) because it has only one cause of non-declension, which is definiteness (taʿrīf).

And indeed they ascend with the deed of the servant and they commend it, and when they reach with it what God wills, He reveals to them: 'You are the guardians over My servant, and I am the watcher over what is in his heart. He has not sincerely dedicated his deed to Me, so place it in Sijjīn.'"

The Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 83, verses 29–33:

They are the polytheists of Makkah: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il and their followers. They used to laugh at 'Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab, Bilal and other poor believers, and mock them. It is also said that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) passed by a group of Muslims, and the hypocrites mocked them, laughed and winked at one another. Then they returned to their companions and said, "Today we saw the bald one," and they laughed at him. So this was revealed before 'Ali reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Winking at one another﴾: each of them signals to the other with his eyes. ﴿Amused﴾: delighting in mentioning them and mocking them. That is, they attribute misguidance to the Muslims. ﴿They were not sent as guardians over them﴾: not appointed to watch over them, to keep account of their conditions, to oversee their deeds, and to bear witness to their rectitude and their error, and to guide them. Or it is part of the words of the disbelievers: when they saw the Muslims, they said, "Indeed, these people are misguided," and "they were not sent as guardians over them," as a denial of the Muslims' efforts to turn them away from polytheism, their call to Islam, and their earnestness in that.

Thawwaba and athaba have the same meaning: to reward, when one repays someone. Aws said:

"I will repay you, or a repayer will repay you on my behalf, and it is enough for you that they praise you and you are commended."

It is said that thawwaba and athaba mean to reward. So al-mathwab (the one rewarded) is the one repaid: "I will repay you, O my horse, with myself, or someone other than me will repay you in my stead." Or it is a reward arising from me, and what suffices you from people is that they praise and commend you. So "fa-alayka" (then upon you) is the deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il). It is also permissible that al-mathwab is the one summoned to battle, signalling with the edge of his garment so that he may be seen from afar and aided.

It is also read with the assimilation of the lām into the tā'.
